clue.text: Contrived neologisms bringing misery

indicators.note: something contrived is artificially arranged, so the letters are put together in a new order

parts.note: taken as written; newly coined words supply all ten letters

explanation.surface: Someone groans at clumsy made-up words that make reading miserable.
explanation.walkthrough: The ten letters of the coined-words noun rearrange exactly into GLOOMINESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloominess is a state of low spirits and sadness, a straightforward synonym for wretched unhappiness.

clue.text: German tree that's cut

parts.note: G is the standard abbreviation for German
the ash is a common tree

explanation.surface: A German tree has been felled or lopped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' reads as a past participle describing the tree, but it is a noun naming a wound.
explanation.definitionFit: A gash is a long deep wound or slash, so it is a noun sense of a cut in skin or material.

clue.text: Lounges not opening for louts

indicators.note: without its opening means the first letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: to loaf is to lounge about idly

explanation.surface: Bars that stay closed to keep out hooligans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lounges' looks like a noun for bars or sofas, but it is the verb: LOAFS, which loses its L to leave OAFS.
explanation.definitionFit: Oafs and louts are both clumsy, boorish, ill-mannered men; the two words are near synonyms.

clue.text: Very fast with classic greeting, Lord Lieutenant is not half conniving type

parts.note: Mach 1, written with Roman I, is the speed of sound
ave is the Latin word of greeting
LL is the abbreviation for Lord Lieutenant

indicators.note: keeping only half of a two-letter word leaves just its first letter

parts.note: half of the two-letter word

explanation.surface: A dignitary rushes in with an old-fashioned salute, half-hearted and scheming.
explanation.walkthrough: Mach one is the speed of sound, with the one written as Roman I. A Lord Lieutenant is the monarch's representative in a British county.
explanation.definitionFit: Niccolò Machiavelli wrote The Prince, and his name became shorthand for a cunning, unscrupulous political schemer.

clue.text: Kind son re-fitted safer kind of tyres

indicators.note: fitted again means reassembled differently, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A thoughtful son put new, safer tyres on a parent's car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind' looks like a description of the son, but its letters are part of the raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: Non-skid tyres have treads designed to grip the road and resist sliding, which makes them safer.

clue.text: Therapists' contracts

definitions.note: plural noun; the possessive is surface only
definitions.meaning: first meaning: slang for psychiatrists or psychotherapists
second meaning: becomes smaller, as a verb

explanation.surface: The legal agreements signed by a group of therapists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contracts' reads as a noun for agreements owned by the therapists; it is really a verb meaning gets smaller.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrink is slang from 'headshrinker' for a psychiatrist, and to shrink is to become smaller in size.

clue.text: In conversation, all initially relieved by Everyman giving promise to pay late

indicators.note: being relieved by someone means handing your post over to them, so one letter takes another's place

parts.note: a chat is an informal talk

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word

parts.note: the opening letter, which is swapped out
the setter refers to himself, so 'Everyman' is I

explanation.surface: A chat in which everyone's worries are eased by the setter offering an IOU.
explanation.walkthrough: In CHAT the A is replaced by I, giving CHIT. The setter's name stands for 'me', so it gives I.
explanation.definitionFit: A chit is a signed note recording a small debt, an informal IOU to be settled later.

clue.text: In the U.S., aim to alter history, etc.

indicators.note: altering something changes its form, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written, ignoring punctuation

explanation.surface: Americans are accused of trying to rewrite the past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the U.S.' looks like setting the scene, but every letter of it is fodder alongside 'aim'.
explanation.definitionFit: History belongs to the humanities, the academic subjects such as literature and philosophy; 'etc.' signals the wider group.

clue.text: Rest day arranged with bed and cuddly companions

indicators.note: arranging things puts them into a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lazy day off spent in bed with soft toys for company.
explanation.walkthrough: Both the rest day and the bed supply letters, combined before rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: Teddy bears are soft toys that children hug, so they are fluffy friends to snuggle.

clue.text: In tent, forces on manoeuvres finding kind of chocolate

indicators.note: troops on manoeuvres move around into new positions

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Soldiers on exercise discover a box of chocolates in their tent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' sets the scene only; the tent and the forces both go into the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A soft centre is a chocolate with a creamy or fondant filling, one variety in a selection box.

clue.text: Surrounded by flipping dull Austria

parts.note: A is the international vehicle code for Austria

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, back to front

parts.note: dim means dull, lacking brightness

explanation.surface: Someone feels trapped in a thoroughly boring Austria.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British expletive intensifying 'dull'; it turns that word around.
explanation.definitionFit: Amid is a preposition meaning in the middle of, encircled or enclosed by other things.

clue.text: Abundance, supply: holy, kind — Amen

indicators.note: read as the adverb of supple, it means in a flexible, bending way

parts.note: taken as written, ignoring punctuation

explanation.surface: A prayer for plenty, asking a holy and kind provider, ending with Amen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like a noun meaning provision; read as 'supple-ly', it is the signal to bend the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A land flowing with milk and honey is the biblical promised land, so the phrase stands for plenty and prosperity.

clue.text: That man's attention is on capital investments?

parts.note: he is the pronoun for that man
to pay one's addresses is to pay courtship attentions

explanation.surface: A financier is focused on investing money in a capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital investments' sounds financial, but capital means head and to invest is to clothe, so the definition is items worn on the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Invest once meant to dress or robe someone, and the capital is the head, so these are ornate coverings worn on top.

clue.text: Ultimately daring, tucking in to the French duck, briefly flambé meaty hunks

indicators.note: said briefly, a word is cut short at its end
to tuck into something is to slip inside it

parts.note: les is the French plural for 'the'

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is wanted

parts.note: final letter
a duck is a zero score in cricket, shaped like O
the French word missing its accented last letter

explanation.surface: A bold cook, tucking into French duck, quickly flames some big cuts of meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' looks like the bird being cooked, but it gives O, a nil score in cricket. The italics on flambé mark it as a French word, here cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: A leg of lamb is a large joint of roasting meat, so several of them are substantial chunks of flesh.

clue.text: Near Cram finally, Coe's overtaking: Cram's first runner-up?

indicators.note: to overtake is to pass round the outside, so one piece ends up enclosing another

parts.note: Sebastian Coe, the British middle-distance runner

indicators.note: finally points to the very last letter of the name

parts.note: last letter of the surname

indicators.note: first points to the opening letter of the name

parts.note: first letter of the surname
the runner-up loses the race

explanation.surface: Steve Cram is just behind as Coe overtakes him; is Cram the runner-up?
explanation.walkthrough: Coe and Cram were rival British middle-distance runners of the 1980s. 'Near' looks like an adjective, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To near something is to approach it, to draw towards it, which is the imperative phrase used as a verb.

clue.text: Turned right away, or changed gradually

indicators.note: sent away means removed and no longer present

parts.note: revolved means rotated or turned
R is the abbreviation for right; it is the letter removed

explanation.surface: Someone either swung round and left or slowly altered course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned right' looks like a driving direction, but right is the letter R taken from REVOLVED.
explanation.definitionFit: Species and ideas that evolved developed step by step over time, so they altered slowly.

clue.text: Clever clogs (Sting, that is)

parts.note: to smart is to sting with pain
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: The rock singer Sting is hailed, parenthetically, as a know-all.
explanation.walkthrough: Sting looks like the musician's name, but it is the verb. 'Clever clogs' is a British phrase for a show-off know-it-all.
explanation.definitionFit: A smartie, or smarty, is someone who flaunts their intelligence, a smart alec or know-it-all.

clue.text: Go off with — largely — the quality of a ninja

indicators.note: largely means most but not all, so the final letter goes

parts.note: to go off with something is to steal it
the word cut short

explanation.surface: Someone sneaks off with most of what makes a ninja a ninja.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go off with' is one phrase for STEAL; 'the' then loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ninjas were trained in covert, silent movement, so moving unseen and unheard is their defining trait.

clue.text: Greedy type, earthy, stripped off for artist

indicators.note: to strip something is to peel off its outer layer, so both edges go

parts.note: a hog is a greedy person
the adjective with its outer letters removed

explanation.surface: A greedy, coarse man strips naked to pose for a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stripped off' suggests undressing to model; it removes the first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: William Hogarth was an eighteenth-century English painter and engraver known for satirical series such as A Rake's Progress.

clue.text: Source of venison increasingly florid Earl's swallowed

indicators.note: something swallowed ends up inside whatever swallowed it

parts.note: a florid face is ruddy; more so is redder
E is the abbreviation for Earl

explanation.surface: A nobleman grows ever more flushed after eating game meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Earl's swallowed' reads as the Earl eating; it means the Earl is the one swallowed, so E goes inside REDDER.
explanation.definitionFit: Venison is deer meat, and the red deer is the large species most hunted and farmed for it in Britain.

clue.text: Former Test captain getting boundary, loudly cheer on

parts.note: Joe Root captained England's Test cricket team

indicators.note: loudly means spoken out, so what is heard counts, not the spelling

parts.note: a boundary in cricket scores four runs

explanation.surface: A cricket fan cheers loudly as an ex-England captain hits the ball to the rope.
explanation.walkthrough: A Test is an international cricket match; a ball reaching the boundary rope along the ground scores four runs.
explanation.definitionFit: To root for a team is an idiom meaning to support it and hope it wins, which is cheering it on.

clue.text: According to Spooner, ornamental edging peculiar, needing cash

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the first sounds trade places

parts.note: ornamental edging is a moulding; its opening M sound is traded for the F of the next word
peculiar means funny; its opening F sound is traded for the M of the first word

explanation.surface: Fancy trim for a room turns out strange and expensive.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the M and F sounds of 'moulding funny' and you say 'folding money'.
explanation.definitionFit: Folding money is banknotes as opposed to coins, so it is an informal term for paper currency.

clue.text: What gives seemingly intelligent robotic intonations, primarily?

definitions.text: What gives seemingly intelligent robotic intonations, primarily?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letters are taken

parts.note: opening letters of the four words

explanation.surface: A riddle about what device speaks in a clever-sounding machine voice.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: the initials spell the name, and the clue describes the thing itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Apple's voice assistant answers spoken questions in a synthetic voice that seems smart, exactly what the clue describes.

clue.text: Stuart monarch, somewhat mannered

indicators.note: somewhat means to some extent, so only part of the next word is used

parts.note: letters two to five of the word

explanation.surface: A Stuart ruler described as rather affected in behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: The queen sits inside the word that follows the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Queen Anne reigned from 1702 to 1714, the last ruler of the Stuart dynasty in Britain.

clue.text: Recess taken from rap session

indicators.note: taken from means extracted out of the words that follow

parts.note: spans the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A break is called during a rap music recording.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recess' looks like a break from work, but it is an alcove in a building.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is a semicircular vaulted alcove at the end of a church, an architectural niche.

clue.text: Declaration: 'It's a career'

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an open statement of belief
second meaning: a paid occupation requiring training

explanation.surface: Someone announces that this is their line of work.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation dresses the clue as one announcement, but the two halves define the same word separately.
explanation.definitionFit: To profess is to declare openly, so a profession is an avowal; it also names a vocation such as law or medicine.

clue.text: Poet's boring in retirement

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing or going back, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: drab means dull and boring

explanation.surface: A poet who has stopped working has become rather dull.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A bard is a traditional term for a poet, especially Shakespeare, known as the Bard.

clue.text: They dance and sing about Egyptian god's ancestry

parts.note: c. is the abbreviation of circa, meaning about
Horus is the falcon-headed Egyptian sky god
a line is a line of descent

explanation.surface: Performers celebrate in song and dance the lineage of an ancient deity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a word meaning concerning, but it gives C for circa.
explanation.definitionFit: A chorus line is the row of supporting performers in a musical who sing and dance together.
